summary: Mission Architect is an interactive 3D spacecraft engineering and orbital operations game where you design a complete space mission from requirements to launch and science operations, balance real aerospace subsystem trade-offs, fly the ascent corridor, and downlink orbital science back to Earth.
details:
Mission Architect is an interactive 3D space-mission engineering and orbital operations game built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge across

four connected phases: assembling a custom spacecraft in a live 3D Vehicle Assembly Bay (selecting from 8 science instruments, spacecraft bus

subsystems, 5 launch vehicles, and 10 orbits across 8 worlds including Earth, the Moon, Venus, Mars, Sun-Earth L2, 16 Psyche, Europa, and

Titan), steering through 3D ascent skyway rings and Max-Q stage separation, operating orbital science via an alternating scan-and-upload loop

inside ground-station and Deep Space Network link cones, and evaluating results against real NASA missions such as Landsat 9, MRO, Magellan,

LRO, and Europa Clipper. Rather than keeping engineering math in a static calculator, the game connects a live Go/No-Go physics and budget

solver directly to 3D flight and orbital gameplay—incorporating emergent subsystem synergies like Edge AI cloud filtering, a 10-mission

campaign, Sandbox mode, an 8-lesson tutorial, and 4-role WebSocket co-op rooms. Its benefit and intended impact are to demystify NASA-style

systems engineering for students, educators, and space enthusiasts by letting them experience how payload choices cascade across mass reserves,

1/r² solar flux versus Pu-238 RTG power, battery Depth of Discharge, pointing precision, radiation tolerance, and downlink bottlenecks.

All code authoring, system architecture, and debugging were performed through the use of SI (Synthetic Intelligence / AI) on a Windows

workstation and LAN-connected WebGL browsers using TypeScript (^5.7.0) in a three-workspace npm monorepo (@mission-architect/sim, @mission-

architect/web, @mission-architect/server) powered by React 18, Three.js (@react-three/fiber and @react-three/drei), Tailwind CSS, Vite, Vitest

(11 simulation unit tests), and a Node.js WebSocket server (ws) paired with structured JSON aerospace catalogs. Grounded in public NASA

references—including NASA Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art reports, Launch Services Program performance data, NTRS technical

papers, and NASA 3D Resources—development focused on balancing simplified Keplerian orbital mechanics, eclipse power budgets, and radiation

models with accessible gameplay across three difficulty levels, a deterministic scan-once/upload-once orbital state machine that prevents

softlocks, lightweight procedural 3D rendering for local-network multiplayer, and strict zero-secret repository hygiene.
